newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen's ruling party ploughs ahead in poll results.
newsitem.headline: Yemen's ruling party ploughs ahead in poll results.

text.p: Yemen's ruling General Peoples Congress (GPC) has swept more than 60 percent of constituencies in counting so far in the poor Arab state's first parliamentary poll since a 1994 civil war, an official said on Wednesday.

The Islah Party, the GPC's junior coalition partner which has accused election supervisors of bias, lagged far behind with less than 20 percent, Saeed al-Hekaimi, spokesman for the Supreme Elections Committee, told a news conference.

President Ali Abdullah Saleh's GPC won 157 out of 247 constituencies counted so far, while Islah controlled only 43, the same number as independent candidates, Hekaimi said. The Nasserite Unionist Party and the Arab Socialist Baath Party each secured two seats in the 301-seat parliament.
Islah earlier on Wednesday accused the Supreme Elections Committee of bias, threatening court action over results of Sunday's poll.

"The Supreme Elections Committee is known to have been biased in favour of one party since the first stage of the elections," Islah's Secretary General Mohammad al-Yadomi said in apparent reference to the GPC.
He said his party would go to court over the alleged bias.
"If the judicial system will not be fair, we will give the seats we won to the GPC," he said. "We will withdraw from the election process without any regrets."
International election observers said on Wednesday the elections appeared to have been reasonably fair considering the country was still experimenting with democracy.
Fre Le Poole, spokeswoman for the Joint International Observer Group in Yemen, said some irregularities noted had been linked to the military.

"The long-term observers noted that, at least in one constituency, a significant number of soldiers were imported and registered in order to vote and thus swing the results in favour...of one candidate," she said without elaborating.
Hekaimi declined to comment on the allegation.
As tension between the ruling parties rose, a security official said four people died in armed clashes between GPC and Islah backers.
The official said the clashes northwest of Sanaa followed a dispute as ballot boxes were being transferred to the capital.
"On their way, they (the two sides) stopped to pray and tensions rose again and they began exchanging fire."

In separate incidents, an election worker died when supporters of independent candidates exchanged fire, while elsewhere a backer of an independent candidate died when a soldier hurled a hand-grenade near a polling station following tension among candidates and supporters, the official said.

The attacks raised the number of deaths in poll-related violence to at least 20, but officials have played down the incidents labelling the attacks criminal. Election observers noted Yemenis often carry weapons.
In united Yemen's first elections in 1993, the GPC won 123 seats, Islah 62 and the Yemen Socialist Party 56. Independents won 47 while the rest went to Baathist and Nasserite parties.
Yemen is the only country in the Arabian peninsula with political parties, opposition newspapers and active Islamist participation in government.
Diplomats describe Yemen's parliament as a pressure group and say power ultimately lies with the president, appointed ministers and military and security forces loyal to the GPC.
